title: Harder sequences
objectives: Find the rule in interleaved, two-step and digit-based sequences.

screens.prose: Trader batteries are reported to include a sequences paper, harder than the 80-in-8 kind. Differences and ratios fail on this one. Look at it in another way.
screens.question: What comes next: 2, 20, 4, 17, 8, 14, 16, ?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the odd places from the even ones.

byKey.odd-half: 32 continues 2, 4, 8, 16. The next place is even, so it continues 20, 17, 14.
byKey.last-minus: You took 3 from the last term, 16. The −3 belongs to the even places: $14 - 3 = 11$.

explain.text: Two sequences take turns: the odd places double, 2, 4, 8, 16, and the even places fall by 3, 20, 17, 14. Place 8 is even, so the answer is 11. Neither rule fits the whole list, which is why differences failed.

screens.prose: Another sequence: 3, 6, 4, 8, 6, 12, 10. Step through the control to see the gaps, then the steps written another way.
screens.question: What comes next?

widget.label: Next term
widget.accept: 20: ×2 and −2 take turns, and ×2 is due.

feedback.correct: 20: the steps take turns, ×2 then −2, and ×2 is next.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Switch the control to steps.

byKey.minus-again: −2 came last. The steps take turns, so ×2 is next: 20.
byKey.gap-rise: You added the last rise, +6. The rises double the term before them: $10 \times 2 = 20$.

explain.text: The gaps +3, +4, +6 look messy, but the steps are just ×2 and −2 taking turns. After a −2 comes a ×2, so 20. Writing each step as an operation, not only a gap, is what found it.

screens.prose: The first sequence was **interleaved**: two sequences in alternate places. The second was **alternating**: two operations taking turns. Try each test on these.

byKey.r2c1: Odd places 40, 38, 36 fall by 2; place 7 is odd: 34. The even places double, but they are not due.

screens.prose: When splitting and steps both fail, look at the digits. The gaps here are 7, 5, 10, 11 and 4. Compare each gap with the term before it.
screens.question: What comes next: 7, 14, 19, 29, 40, 44, ?

hints.text: What are the digits of 14, and what is the gap after it?

feedback.correct: 52: each term adds its own digit sum, and $4 + 4 = 8$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add each term’s digits and compare with the gap.

byKey.repeat-gap: You added the last gap, 4, again. Each gap is the digit sum of the term before: $4 + 4 = 8$, so 52.

explain.text: Each gap is the digit sum of the term before: $7$, $1 + 4$, $1 + 9$, $2 + 9$, $4 + 0$. So the next gap is $4 + 4 = 8$, giving 52. No difference or ratio rule could find that.

screens.prose: Some digit rules are about the words. Each term here describes the one before it, read aloud.
screens.question: What comes next: 1, 11, 21, 1211, 111221, ?

hints.text: Read 111221 aloud in groups of equal digits.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the last term aloud as groups of equal digits.

byKey.too-far: 13112221 reads 312211 aloud: you went one term too far.

explain.text: 111221 reads as three 1s, two 2s, one 1. Written down, that is 312211. Number size is no help here: only reading the digits finds it.

screens.prose: A candidate sees 2, 4, 8 and starts doubling. Check every term before you commit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test your rule on every term, then split the places.

byKey.doubling: You doubled from the first three terms. The fourth term, 6, breaks that rule.
byKey.even-half: 10 continues the even places 4, 6, 8. Place 7 is odd.
byKey.double-32: The odd places multiply by 4, not 2: 2, 8, 32, then 128.

explain.text: Doubling fits 2, 4, 8 and fails at 6. Split, the odd places are 2, 8, 32 and the even places 4, 6, 8. Place 7 is odd, so 128.

screens.prose: Some sequences fit two rules. 1, 2, 4 doubles to 8, but its gaps +1, +2 also suggest +3, giving 7. Graded drills here use only sequences with one clear rule; a real test may not.
screens.question: A test shows 1, 2, 4, ? and offers both 7 and 8. What do you do?

options.text: Give 8, the simplest rule, and move on
Work out every rule that fits before answering
options.why: Three terms fit many rules. Listing them all costs the time of a whole question.

options.text: Leave it blank, since it is ambiguous
options.why: A forward-only test may not allow a blank, and with no penalty a blank wastes a free guess.

options.text: Give 7, since tests like a twist
options.why: Tests mark the simplest rule. Nothing in three terms favours the twist.

hints.text: Doubling is one operation; growing gaps is a rule about a rule.

feedback.correct: Give 8 and move on: one operation beats a rule about gaps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the simplest rule and keep your pace.

byKey.all: Three terms fit many rules. Listing them all costs the time of a whole question.
byKey.blank: A forward-only test may not allow a blank, and with no penalty a blank wastes a free guess.
byKey.twist: Tests mark the simplest rule. Nothing in three terms favours the twist.

explain.text: When two rules fit, give the one with fewer parts and move on. Doubling is one operation; growing gaps is a rule about the gaps. Spending 30 s on the choice costs more than the mark is worth.

screens.prose: When differences and ratios fail, you split the places, wrote each step, then read the digits. Interleaved means two sequences: $$a_1, a_3, a_5, \dots \quad \text{and} \quad a_2, a_4, a_6, \dots$$ Alternating means $a_{n+1} = f(a_n)$ and $g(a_n)$ in turn.

screens.prose: Put the tests in the order to try them, quickest and most common first. Leave out the habit that gives wrong answers.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Differences: gaps, then gaps of gaps, until a row is constant
Ratios: divide each term by the last, perhaps with a fixed step
Interleaved: split odd and even places and solve each half
Alternating: write each step as an operation and look for a pair taking turns
Digit rules: digit sums, reversals, reading the digits aloud
Stop at the first rule that fits the first three terms
lines.why: Three terms fit many rules: 2, 4, 8 went on to 6. Test the rule on every term.

hints.text: Arithmetic tests first, digit tests last.
Splitting comes before writing each step.
Differences, ratios, interleaved, alternating, digit rules.

feedback.correct: Differences, ratios, interleaved, alternating, then digit rules.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the tests from level 3, then the new ones.

byKey.d1: Three terms fit many rules: 2, 4, 8 went on to 6. Test the rule on every term.
byKey.left-out: Every line except stopping at three terms belongs.
byKey.s3: Splitting comes after differences and ratios, which are quicker to write.
byKey.s4: Writing each step comes after splitting, which needs no working.
byKey.s5: Digit rules come last: they are the rarest and the slowest to test.

explain.text: Differences and ratios settle most sequences in seconds. Splitting and stepping catch the two-rule kinds. Digit rules are rare, so they come last.

screens.title: Splitting in code
screens.prose: `split_interleaved(seq)` returns the odd places and the even places as two lists. `next_term(seq)` tries differences, then a constant ratio, then both halves. A half counts if differences or a ratio solve it; both must. It returns `None` if nothing fits.
screens.question: Complete `next_term`; `split_interleaved` and the two simple tests are written.

widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests, compared exactly: three simple sequences, six interleaved ones, three it should not solve (digit sums, alternating steps, factorials), and one split.

hints.text: Call the simple tests on the whole sequence first.
If they fail, split the sequence and run the simple tests on each half.
With an even length the next place is odd, so it continues the first half.

feedback.correct: `next_term` solves the interleaved sequences and refuses the rest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try the whole sequence first, then both halves, and pick the half that holds the next place.

explain.text: A sequence of even length ends on an even place, so the next term is odd and continues the first half. Alternating steps and digit sums return `None`: those stay your job. 12, 21, 23, 32, 34, 43 splits cleanly, so 45 comes out either way.

screens.title: Drill: six sequences
screens.prose: Six sequences, each with one clear rule. Target: about 30 seconds each, 3 minutes in all. Use your own watch; the app does not time you. Run the tests in order.
screens.question: Fill in the next term of each.

hints.text: The second doubles its gaps; the fourth is $2^n + 1$.

feedback.correct: All six. Note your time against 3 minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows.

byKey.r5c1: Reverse, then add 2: 43 reversed is 34, so +2 gives 45.

explain.text: Two rows doubled their gaps, one used a growing ratio, and one was interleaved. The last reverses then adds 2; its halves also climb by 11. When two readings agree, answer at once.

screens.question: If the pattern holds, what size is quoted at level 7?

ideas: When differences and ratios fail, split odd and even places, then write each step as an operation.

Test a rule on every term, and give the simplest rule when two fit.
